THIS CRIMINAL MISC. CASE HAVING BEEN FINALLY HEARD ON 25.11.2025, THE COURT ON 27.11.2025 PASSED THE FOLLOWING:
Ajish Babu V vs Food Safety Officer on 27 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/68230884/

entities.text: Ajish Babu V vs Food Safety Officer on 27 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The petitioners are the accused Nos.1 and 2 in C.C No.45/2019 on the files of the Chief Judicial Magistrate Court, Thrissur.
The first petitioner is stated to be a food business operator who conducts the second petitioner firm, which is a hyper market functioning at Thrissur.

The petitioners were booked by the Food Safety Officer, Thrissur Circle, for violation of Sections 27, 59(1), 52 and 3(1)(zz)(v)(viii), 3.1(zf)(C)(i) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and Regulations 2.2.2:4 and 2.2.2:6 of Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: 2. The allegation against the petitioners is that the first petitioner stored unsafe and misbranded baby rusk for sale in the second petitioner hypermarket firm.
The Food Safety Officer, Thrissur Circle is said to have inspected the second petitioner hypermarket firm and took the samples of packed baby rusk, which were found to be misbranded.

The aforesaid baby rusk, upon analysis at the Regional Analytical Laboratory, Ernakulam, were found to have contained synthetic food colour,
tartrazine, in contravention of Regulation 3.1.2:6 2025:KER:90999 of Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011 which was unsafe as per Section 3.1.(zz)(vii) of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: At the request of the third accused/ manufacturer, one sample of the food item was sent for analysis at the Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore.
However, the certificate issued from the said Laboratory also confirmed the findings of the Regional Analytical Laboratory.
3. In the present petition, the petitioners would contend that the prosecution initiated against them is totally unsustainable.
It is stated that the food analysis was not done in accordance with the standing rules.
According to the petitioners, they cannot be held liable for misbranding of packaged food commodities sold to them by the manufacturer.
It is further contended that the findings in the laboratory test cannot be attributed any value since the food item was not toasted bread.

4. Heard the learned counsel for the petitioners, the learned Additional Director General of Prosecution representing respondents 1 and 2, and the learned Public Prosecutor representing the State of Kerala.

As regards the allegation of misbranding, it is argued by the learned counsel for the petitioners that they cannot be held liable for the above violation since the food item involved was a packaged commodity.
According to the petitioners, the manufacturer alone can be held liable for the above violation of law.

6. The argument advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioner in the above regard cannot be accepted in view of the provisions contained in Section 26 of the Food Safety and Standards Act,
Ajish Babu V vs Food Safety Officer on 27 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/68230884/
2 2006 dealing with the responsibilities of the food business operator.

entities.text: Ajish Babu V vs Food Safety Officer on 27 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
As per the above provision of law, every food business operator shall ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of the said Act, and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder, at all stages of production,
processing, import, distribution and sale.

Going by the definition of 'Food Business Operator' and 'Food Business' in Section 3(o) and 3(n) respectively of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the seller would also come under the definition of food business operator.
Therefore, the petitioners cannot be heard to say that they are not liable to be prosecuted for selling misbranded packaged 2025:KER:90999 commodities of food in their establishment.

Even otherwise, a defence in the above regard is a matter to be considered during trial, and that cannot be a reason to exercise the inherent powers of this Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C, to terminate the prosecution at the very inception.

7. The learned counsel for the petitioners, by relying on Annexure-A3 order of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India argued that, as per the instructions issued thereunder, the analysis by way of DGHS method as done by the Referral Laboratory, Mysore and the Regional Analytical Laboratory, Ernakulam, were against the standing instructions.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Thus, it is pointed out that the authorities concerned erred in complying with the rules with regard to the way in which the food items are to be analysed.
There is no merit in the above argument of the learned counsel for the petitioners.
What is stated in Annexure-A3 order is that the FSSAI Manual of Method of Analysis shall be used by the laboratories with immediate effect.

entities.text: FSSAI Manual of Method of Analysis
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: The learned Additional Director General of Prosecution has filed the communication issued by the Referral Food Laboratory, Mysore, which would reveal that the DGHS Manual being followed for 2025:KER:90999 the analysis of food by the laboratories are basically the same in procedure and technique as that of FSSAI Manual of Method for Food Additives.

entities.text: FSSAI Manual of Method for Food Additives
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid communication, it cannot be said that the food analysis in the case on hand was conducted in violation of the standing instructions.

8. Another argument advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioners is that the synthetic colour tartrazine found to have been added to the food item, cannot be considered as an additive,
not permitted by the relevant Rules and Regulations.
According to the petitioners, tartrazine is permitted to be used in the bread products as per Appendix-A, Table 7 under the food category 7.2.1.
The contention of the petitioners in the above regard, is totally unfounded.

As per Appendix-A,
Table 7 under the food category 7.2.1, the additives mentioned in Column No.3 could be used only for cakes, cookies, biscuits, crackers and pies.

The food product rusk comes under the category 7.1.4 under the heading 'Bread-type products, including bread stuffing and bread crumbs' which include bread based products such as croutons, bread stuffing and stuffing mixes, and prepared doughs like toasted bread, rusks prepared doughs for 2025:KER:90999 bread/bread-type products including their frozen counterparts etc.

The additive tartrazine is not included in Column No.3 of the list of additives under Appendix-A, Table 7 and food category 7.1.4, which deals with bread-type products including bread stuffing and bread crumbs.
Therefore, the argument advanced in the above regard by the learned counsel for the petitioners, cannot be accepted.
9. The complaint and accompanying records relied on by the prosecution are capable of prima facie showing that the petitioners committed the offences alleged against them in this case.

Therefore, it is not possible to terminate the prosecution proceedings against them, in exercise of the powers of Ajish Babu V vs Food Safety Officer on 27 November, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/68230884/
3 this Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C.

sentences.text: Needless to say, the prayer in this petition to quash the proceedings against the petitioners, cannot be allowed.
In the result, the petition is hereby dismissed.
